tip: To give your name, Russian says зовут (zovut = they call) plus you in the object form: Меня (Menya = me). It reads 'me they-call'.
Днём (Dnyom = in the daytime) is the instrumental form used for time of day; the -ём (-yom) ending means 'during', no preposition needed.
To ask the time, Russian says Который час (Kotoryy chas = which hour), literally 'which hour', not 'what time'.
свою (svoyu = one's own) points back to the subject, so it fits any person. Use it, not мою (moyu = my), when the owner is the subject.
To say you speak a language, use the по- adverb: по-русски (po-russki = in Russian). Lowercase and hyphenated, not the noun form.
нет (net = there isn't) forces the next noun into the genitive: телефона (telefona = of a phone). It marks the missing thing.
The tool you use goes in the instrumental with no preposition: левой рукой (levoy rukoy = with the left hand). The -ой (-oy) ending means 'by means of'.
The -ся (-sya) on закрывается (zakryvaetsya = closes) makes it happen by itself; the museum does not close something, it just closes.
The person you write to goes in the dative: другу (drugu = to a friend). No separate word for 'to'; the -у (-u) ending carries it.
For an animate male object, accusative copies the genitive: хорошего стоматолога (khoroshego stomatologa = a good dentist). The -ого/-а (-ogo/-a) endings mark it.
заниматься (zanimat'sya = to be occupied with) takes the instrumental, so 'what' becomes чем (chem): чем я занимаюсь (chem ya zanimayus' = what I do).
Age puts the person in the dative and drops the verb 'to be': Бабушке (Babushke = to grandmother) is eighty-five, literally 'to grandmother 85'.
Feeling hot or cold uses the dative and no verb 'to be': Мне (Mne = to me) жарко (zharko = hot) means 'I am hot'.
около (okolo = about) gives an approximate time or amount and takes the genitive: около двух часов (okolo dvukh chasov = about two hours).
Minutes 'to' the hour use без (bez = without) plus the genitive: Без десяти два (Bez desyati dva = ten to two), literally 'without ten, two'.
To say how long an action took to finish, use за (za = in) plus the accusative: за час (za chas = in an hour).
For an action still going on, Russian keeps the present where English uses 'have been': жду уже (zhdu uzhe = I've already been waiting).
Зачем (Zachem = what for) asks about purpose, while почему (pochemu = why) asks about cause. Here it means 'what do you need it for'.
A date you do something 'on' takes the genitive: Второго февраля (Vtorogo fevralya = on the second of February). No word for 'on' needed.
едет (edet = is riding) is one trip happening right now; ездит (ezdit = rides) would mean regular, repeated trips.
After 2, 3, 4 the noun is genitive singular, not plural: четыре книги (chetyre knigi = four books).
Working 'as' a profession uses the instrumental: работает врачом (rabotaet vrachom = works as a doctor). The -ом (-om) ending replaces 'as a'.
For 'on' recurring days, use по (po) plus the dative: по выходным (po vykhodnym = on weekends). It marks a repeated schedule.
After говорите (govorite = you speak), a language takes the по- adverb: по-английски (po-angliyski), по-русски (po-russki), not the noun form.
'By' a vehicle uses на (na) plus the prepositional: на велосипеде (na velosipede = by bicycle). Same на (na) as 'on', different job.
помогать (pomogat' = to help) takes a dative object with no 'to': помогает младшему (pomogaet mladshemu = helps the younger one), with the -ему (-emu) ending.
The pair ни...ни (ni...ni = neither...nor) still needs не (ne) on the verb: не хочу (ne khochu = I don't want). Russian keeps both negatives.
After с (s = with), the noun goes instrumental: с которой (s kotoroy = with whom). которой is the instrumental of который (kotoryy = which).
Откуда (Otkuda = from where) asks origin, unlike где (gde = where) for location and куда (kuda = where to) for destination.
'Than anyone' after a comparative is just the genitive: усерднее всех (userdneye vsekh = harder than everyone). No separate word for 'than'.
которую (kotoruyu = which) is feminine to match Книга (Kniga = book), but accusative because it is the object of прочитал (prochital = read).
